item.title: Update: ConnectWise SkyKick app credential used in 162+ Microsoft 365 tenants; disabling it does not undo planted access
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, was responsible for the compromise, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants after an automated password spray from the same network range, and warns that credential changes planted in tenants can persist after the vendor application is remediated. ConnectWise itself says it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21.
item.content:encoded:
Update22 Oct 2026 03:46 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelbodyentitiesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummary

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, was responsible for the compromise, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants after an automated password spray from the same network range, and warns that credential changes planted in tenants can persist after the vendor application is remediated. ConnectWise itself says it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, was responsible for the compromise. It says AI agents running the ARTEX framework kept signing in to customer tenants as the ConnectWise applications, without an interactive user sign-in, and in multiple tenants went on to Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to change privileges (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). It counts attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants at up to 2,900 attempts a minute and links the activity to an automated cross-tenant password spray between 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-14 against 327 accounts at eight organizations, from the same network range and including an address that ConnectWise's advisory later listed among its indicators; the spray produced no successful authentication (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Microsoft warns that the application credential changes can remain active as a backdoor after the vendor application is remediated, and asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, together with the Entra audit trail for credential additions, role assignments, consents and owner changes (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Expel, which analysed the activity separately, relays the attribution, notes that ConnectWise's fix leaves secrets planted on other applications in place and that Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record, and says Huntress has not tied its Global Administrator observation to the same operator (Expel, 2026-10-21). ConnectWise itself says that, based on the evidence available to it, including threat intelligence shared by Microsoft, it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and used an openly available agentic AI framework (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21). It began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21, expects it to take several days, says the start of restoration does not mean all capabilities are available, and tells partners to keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to their service, while noting that its actions do not remove unauthorized access already established in individual customer tenants (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21; heise online, 2026-10-21). ConnectWise publishes updates twice daily from 2026-10-22 (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21).

item.title: Group-IB: k0t takes edge devices in bulk and decrypts FortiGate configurations offline; enable private-data-encryption
item.description: Group-IB and NyxLab report a campaign by an operator they track as k0t that finds exposed FortiGate, FortiWeb and PAN-OS GlobalProtect devices in bulk, exploits FortiWeb CVE-2025-64446 and GlobalProtect CVE-2026-0257 or brute-forces FortiGate logins, downloads each FortiGate configuration and decrypts its stored LDAP, Active Directory and administrator secrets offline with the default FortiOS key, which cannot be seen on the appliance. Group-IB then sees hands-on Active Directory work, remote-management persistence and exfiltration, and victims that later appear on the Qilin and The Gentlemen leak sites; it assesses the operators as probable initial-access brokers but says the link to either group is unconfirmed.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2025-64446 +2exploitedNATOB2

k0t: Group-IB and NyxLab describe a probable access broker that mass-exploits FortiWeb and PAN-OS GlobalProtect, brute-forces FortiGate and decrypts stolen FortiGate configurations offline with the default key, with victims later listed by Qilin and The Gentlemen

Group-IB and NyxLab describe a campaign by an operator they track as k0t (Group-IB lists CryptoFeel as a potential alias, and Scrooge as a likely collaborator and possible alias) that enumerates internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances in bulk and attacks the product directly, chiefly Fortinet firewalls and Palo Alto GlobalProtect portals (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). A custom script exploits CVE-2025-64446 against FortiWeb, a relative path traversal that lets an unauthenticated attacker run administrative commands, or brute-forces exposed Fortinet devices as a fallback (Group-IB, 2026-10-21; CISA KEV, 2026-10-21). Against PAN-OS it exploits CVE-2026-0257, the GlobalProtect authentication bypass, with a forged authentication-override cookie (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). On a compromised FortiGate the tool downloads the configuration and decrypts its secrets locally with the default FortiOS key, the weakness tracked as CVE-2019-6693, recovering LDAP and Active Directory bind and, Group-IB says, administrator credentials, although Fortinet's advisory excludes the administrator's password and says FIPS-CC devices are not impacted; unless private-data-encryption is set, the device falls back to that known key (Group-IB, 2026-10-21; Fortinet, 2019-11-19).

After access the operators work by hand with NetExec, Impacket, Kerbrute, relayed PetitPotam and Mimikatz, keep access through OpenConnect, MeshCentral agents, AdaptixC2, Atera and AnyDesk, and exfiltrate with Rclone to Wasabi and MEGA (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). Group-IB sees victim overlap with the Qilin and The Gentlemen leak sites and assesses the operators are probably initial-access brokers, but says no relationship is confirmed, and it found indications of a possible connection with the FortiBleed cluster alongside negligible overlap in the compromised credentials (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). CISA lists all three CVEs in KEV, with ransomware use marked known for CVE-2026-0257 and CVE-2019-6693 (CISA KEV, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Internet-reachable FortiGate administrator and VPN logins, FortiWeb up to 8.0.1, 7.6.4, 7.4.9, 7.2.11 or 7.0.11 on its branch (Fortinet, 2025-11-14), and PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways below the per-branch fixed builds (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-05-13); every FortiGate except FIPS-CC models is exposed to the offline decryption step once its configuration has been downloaded unless private-data-encryption, available from FortiOS 5.6.11, 6.0.7 and 6.2.1 and off by default, is enabled with an operator-defined key, which Fortinet warns can cause install errors and split-brain on FortiManager-managed or HA FortiGates until FortiManager 6.2.7 and FortiGate 6.2.6, 6.4.4 or 6.6.0 and later (Group-IB, 2026-10-21; Fortinet, 2019-11-19).
Detection
On edge appliances, unexpected local administrator creation, configuration exports, trusted-host changes, repeated authentication failures, lockout-and-retry patterns and administration from unusual source addresses; on directory infrastructure, the NetExec, Impacket and relay pattern against domain controllers; on endpoints, remote-management agents and dual-use tools without an approved owner. The decryption leaves no trace on the appliance, so a patched or cleaned device may already have yielded its secrets (Group-IB, 2026-10-21). After upgrading FortiWeb, Fortinet advises reviewing configuration and logs for unexpected changes and unauthorised administrator accounts, and until then disabling HTTP and HTTPS on internet-facing interfaces (Fortinet, 2025-11-14).

Triage: OpenConnect, MeshCentral, Atera, AnyDesk and Rclone are legitimate tools, so Group-IB advises judging execution context, installation source, operator account, destination and timing rather than tool names (Group-IB, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Enable private-data-encryption with an operator-defined key on every FortiGate and rotate the directory and administrator secrets stored in any configuration that may have left the device, because patching or rebuilding does not undo a copy already decrypted; Group-IB also advises investigating lockout events and raising the lockout time against brute force (Group-IB, 2026-10-21).

item.title: Update: PHP2Shell: fixed PHP builds are out and attack traffic is already hitting unpatched servers; update the runtime, not the CMS
item.description: The fixed releases (PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35) shipped on 2026-10-21, so the earlier no-fix status ends; Cloudflare, watchTowr and VulnCheck report attack traffic and at least one unsuccessful web-shell attempt, proofs of concept are circulating, VulnCheck holds an exploit that succeeds with ASLR enabled and no source reports a confirmed compromise, so priority moves to critical. Swiss cantons, universities, the Lodur fire-brigade platform and Publica took sites offline as a precaution, and BACS, CERT-EU and ENISA tell operators to update the runtime, check embedded installations and look for compromise.
item.content:encoded:
Update22 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelactionsbodyclassificationconfidencecvesevidenceheadlineimmediate_actionpriorityregionssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

The fixed releases (PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35) shipped on 2026-10-21, so the earlier no-fix status ends; Cloudflare, watchTowr and VulnCheck report attack traffic and at least one unsuccessful web-shell attempt, proofs of concept are circulating, VulnCheck holds an exploit that succeeds with ASLR enabled and no source reports a confirmed compromise, so priority moves to critical. Swiss cantons, universities, the Lodur fire-brigade platform and Publica took sites offline as a precaution, and BACS, CERT-EU and ENISA tell operators to update the runtime, check embedded installations and look for compromise.

The fixed releases shipped on 2026-10-21 between 13:30 and 14:00 UTC, depending on the source, together with the technical advisories, so the earlier statement that no fix existed no longer holds (CERT-EU, 2026-10-21; ENISA, 2026-10-21; Sansec, 2026-10-21). ENISA, the European Commission, CERT-EU, Europol EC3 and the CSIRTs network advise organisations to identify their PHP-based applications, coordinate with hosting and service providers, apply the update to internet-facing systems first, and isolate exposed applications from public networks where that is not possible (ENISA, 2026-10-21). BACS published its warning the same day, telling operators to check embedded and internal PHP installations as well as public sites, to restart long-running PHP processes and rebuild containers, to verify the running version, and, where an immediate update is impossible, to consider disconnecting critical applications from the internet (BACS, 2026-10-21). BACS told RTS it knows of no reliable, confirmed substitute for the updates and that the interim measures give no guaranteed full protection (RTS, 2026-10-21).

Attack traffic was reported on the day: Cloudflare saw it against its customers while the flaws were still leaked, watchTowr's honeypots recorded exploitation, and VulnCheck's canary hosts logged scanning from 08:37 UTC and at least one unsuccessful web-shell attempt through a session file, while VulnCheck says it holds a working exploit for CVE-2026-109618 that succeeds on x86-64 with ASLR enabled; no source reports a confirmed compromise (Cloudflare, 2026-10-21; watchTowr, 2026-10-21; VulnCheck, 2026-10-21). Palo Alto Networks confirmed that every PAN-OS and Panorama release is affected through the management web interface, with no fixed release yet (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).

Public-sector sites went offline as a precaution, mostly on the evening of 2026-10-21. The canton of Basel-Stadt activated its crisis staff and shut down every PHP-run cantonal website with no restoration time given, while stating that no security-relevant incident had been registered (Canton of Basel-Stadt, 2026-10-21). The Ticino cantonal administration temporarily disabled some online services, the website of the University of Geneva was unreachable, and the EPFL site displayed a notice that its pages were currently unreachable, although nau.ch says it still worked (nau.ch, 2026-10-21); RTS lists the EPFL and University of Geneva sites as temporarily suspended (RTS, 2026-10-21). Several Neuchâtel canton and city sites were unreachable without an official statement; Arcinfo presumes a link to the PHP flaw, which the state had not confirmed (RTS, 2026-10-21). Lodur, the platform many Swiss fire brigades use to manage their fire brigades and alarm groups, was out of service because its provider took its servers offline as a precaution: users could neither read stored data nor edit alarm groups, though the Valais cantonal fire office said this does not necessarily mean the alarm-triggering systems are down (nau.ch, 2026-10-21; RTS, 2026-10-21). Publica took its website offline on the afternoon of 2026-10-21 as a precaution, says it has closed the vulnerabilities with security updates and was back online that evening, and states the outage is unrelated to the cyberattack on its software supplier (Publica, 2026-10-21). Dutch authorities took DigiD, MijnOverheid, Overheid.nl, TweedeKamer.nl and the tax authority offline for a time, and most were back by that evening (Security.nl, 2026-10-21); RTS reports that the site of the Paris police prefecture was also suspended (RTS, 2026-10-21). Basel-Stadt said it would report on progress on the morning of 2026-10-22, and no restoration status had been published as of the early morning of 2026-10-22 UTC.

Open finding: CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, PHP (PHP2Shell): two unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaws in the runtime, fixed on 2026-10-21 in 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, with attack traffic already observed and no upstream release for 8.1 and older (CVSS 4.0 9.2) →

item.title: Microsoft: Storm-0940 runs the ARTEX agent framework at machine speed; Expel adds an Okta self-registration technique
item.description: Microsoft reports that since at least September 2026 Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, has used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework, to automate scanning, password spraying and OAuth-application abuse against hundreds of organizations across many industries including government, reaching privileged cloud access in under three hours in several cases. Expel independently saw the same infrastructure create its own accounts through Okta self-service registration, enrol Okta Verify and sign in to applications, and CrowdStrike and Recorded Future document another actor using the same framework.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB2

ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that as early as September 2026 Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, used the agentic penetration-testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations across many industries, government and military among them (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent LLM system that can use any AI model and runs a penetration test from reconnaissance to exfiltration with little human involvement (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Microsoft says ARTEX accelerated the abuse of compromised applications already granted access to Microsoft 365 tenants (Microsoft, 2026-10-21), and Expel adds that it is not a vulnerability and only speeds up familiar techniques such as password spraying and OAuth-application abuse (Expel, 2026-10-21); most targeting failed, yet several cases went from first targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Microsoft assesses the same actor was behind the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application-credential abuse (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Expel saw Storm-0940 infrastructure scan a customer and, from 2026-10-13, abuse its Okta self-service registration with no ConnectWise application involved: the attacker created five accounts of its own, enrolled Okta Verify on three of them about a minute after activation, made 50 single sign-on logins with more than 100 OAuth tokens issued and ran a password spray that Okta ThreatInsight blocked (Expel, 2026-10-21). Expel says the shared source address is its only link to Storm-0940, the activity alone does not prove ARTEX was used, and it had not seen the technique reported before (Expel, 2026-10-21). Other actors use it: CrowdStrike analysed an unnamed, probably Chinese-speaking and financially motivated actor that ran ARTEX against South Korean financial institutions from late September (CrowdStrike, 2026-10-07), and Recorded Future, which tracks that activity as TAG-217, says use of ARTEX and other AI penetration-testing tools is not limited to it (Recorded Future, 2026-10-16).

Wiz Research independently reports that throughout October 2026 it tracked an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors, focused on identity providers (Okta, Entra, Cognito) and Microsoft 365 integrations, and says that most attempts failed and that none of the techniques is novel (Wiz, 2026-10-22). It describes a consistent sequence: downloading JavaScript bundles, exposed source maps, runtime configuration and OpenAPI documents, then calling internal API routes by name minutes later; fabricated authorization codes and malformed state values against Microsoft OAuth callbacks; unsigned JWTs tried against more than 60 SSO route variants in two minutes; and account-recovery, sign-up and Cognito calls such as InitiateAuth, ForgotPassword and ResendConfirmationCode (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Its password sprays against Entra and Okta hit hundreds of users, mainly software engineers, in bursts of 20 to 60 minutes with a unique user agent per burst, a median gap of one second between attempts and new source addresses within minutes of a block (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Exposure
Any tenant that relies on password sign-in or grants OAuth consent to applications, and any Okta org with self-service registration enabled; not using ConnectWise does not exclude exposure (Expel, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In the authentication logs of every identity provider in use, bursts of failed logons and lockouts spread over many accounts; in the Okta system log, newly self-registered accounts that enrol Okta Verify and start single sign-on within minutes; and in the Entra audit log, credentials or certificates added to applications that nobody on your team created and any application that assigns itself a directory role (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21). A clean audit log is not proof of no access, because Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record (Expel, 2026-10-21). In web access logs of an application exposed to the same actor, Wiz points to source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes that appear only in those files, and to sign-in telemetry showing a new user agent for each burst of attempts at a one-second cadence (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

Triage: Python and curl user agents match common legitimate automation, so Expel treats them as supporting evidence only, and a Python user agent on an application that normally calls Microsoft Graph with a .NET SDK is the anomaly (Expel, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Expel's reading is that the framework adds speed, not a new vulnerability, so the levers are the identity controls it runs into: least privilege on multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants, alerting on credential additions and privileged role assignments by applications, and a review of self-registered Okta accounts since 2026-10-13 (Microsoft, 2026-10-21; Expel, 2026-10-21).
Improvement24 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_note

Wiz Research reports an actor using ARTEX-associated tooling, overlapping with Storm-0940, against IT and software vendors throughout October 2026, focused on Okta, Entra and Cognito and on Microsoft 365 integrations, with most attempts failing (Wiz, 2026-10-22). It describes the log signatures of the agent: source-map and OpenAPI downloads followed minutes later by calls to internal routes that appear only in those files, fabricated OAuth callback values, unsigned JWTs tried against more than 60 SSO route variants in two minutes, account-recovery and sign-up calls, and password-spray bursts of 20 to 60 minutes against Entra and Okta with a unique user agent per burst and a median gap of one second between attempts (Wiz, 2026-10-22). Wiz says chaining, automatic adaptation to rate limits and blocks, and tests against heavily scrutinised Microsoft OAuth flows separate the agent from a human operator (Wiz, 2026-10-22).

item.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI and in the official images stole cloud and AI credentials; removing the package does not stop it
item.description: On 2026-10-21 LiteLLM 1.107.0, the open-source LLM gateway, shipped with malicious Python startup files in all seven PyPI wheels (live 11:39 to 13:23 UTC) and in the official GHCR and Docker Hub images behind the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest and main-stable tags (11:46 to 14:20 UTC); they run a credential stealer at every Python start and start a background loader that could execute code fetched from an attacker-chosen host, though Socket saw its pointer empty at 13:01 UTC. The maintainers' root-cause post of 2026-10-23 says a master key committed to a public repository on 2026-05-27 and never revoked gave the attacker, from 2026-10-10, a GitHub organization owner's CLI token, with which it stole two maintainers' tokens and, on 2026-10-21, overrode branch protection to build the release from a look-alike repository; Socket independently found secret-stealing workflows running on 2026-10-10. Wiz saw stolen AWS instance-role credentials tested about 4.5 hours after exfiltration; PyPI and the registries removed the release the same day and the maintainers say to pin 1.106.2 or an explicit earlier version.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLEupdatedNATOB1

LiteLLM 1.107.0: the PyPI wheels and the official Docker images carried a credential stealer and a dormant remote-code loader that Python starts at every launch, published through the maintainers' own release workflow with stolen developer tokens

Socket reports that LiteLLM 1.107.0, an open-source LLM gateway, carries malicious Python startup files in all seven wheels, and that Upwind found the same payload in the published images (Socket, 2026-10-21). A startup hook and a second startup module in the Python library directory run at every Python start without the application importing LiteLLM: the first collects cloud, Kubernetes, CI, registry and database credentials, SSH, GPG and TLS private keys, browser stores, AI-tool credential files, environment variables and, where configured, the credentials saved in a LiteLLM proxy database; the second forks a detached loader that polls a file in a GitHub repository for a domain and would execute Python downloaded from it with no signature or hash check, though at 13:01 UTC the pointer returned an empty body, which stops the loader before its download stage (Socket, 2026-10-21).

The payload is not in the git tag: a packaging setting in an untagged commit pulls it into the wheel, and the container build provenance records a source repository named Berri-AI/litellm, one hyphen away from BerriAI/litellm (Socket, 2026-10-21). The maintainers' root-cause post of 2026-10-23, which they call the canonical account and which corrects assumptions in their earlier status updates, traces the chain to a configuration file committed on 2026-05-27 to a public repository with the master key of an experimental internal agent service; the commit was force-pushed over but the key was never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-10 the attacker used that key against the service's API, which returned the GitHub CLI OAuth token of an organization owner, not a service account and not scoped down, and from then on the attacker held owner-level access to every repository; such CLI tokens are post-2FA and exempt from GitHub's re-authentication for sensitive actions (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). With it the attacker pushed throwaway branches whose workflows posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint, yielding the CLI tokens of two maintainers, and deleted the workflow runs minutes later (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Socket found secret-exfiltration workflows running in the repository on 2026-10-10 from its Actions performance metrics, eleven days before the release attack, says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access and does not claim that the 2026-10-10 theft produced the access used on 2026-10-21, while LiteLLM says its audit logs tie the token stolen on 2026-10-10 to the approval of the release (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 a push to the private release-orchestration repository with a maintainer's token was rejected by branch protection, and the owner's token then overrode it so that the build could be pointed at the look-alike repository; the owner's token dispatched the staging build, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate, a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, and the owner's token force-pushed the history clean, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). LiteLLM distributes an embargoed release for a vulnerability whose disclosure is scheduled for 2026-10-27 to enterprise customers through a private registry (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21). PyPI quarantined 1.107.0 and the images were pulled the same day (Aikido, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
An environment that installed litellm 1.107.0 from PyPI between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC on 2026-10-21, or pulled the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest or main-stable tag of the official images from GHCR (until about 13:51 UTC) or Docker Hub (until 14:20 UTC); lockfiles, caches, build logs and running image digests show which (Socket, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In the cloud audit logs of every account the host could reach, a caller-identity check followed by a Bedrock model listing and IAM enumeration, made with an instance-role credential harvested from CI runners or Kubernetes nodes from an address outside your estate, which Wiz saw from 16:20 UTC on 2026-10-21 (Wiz, 2026-10-21); on hosts, startup hooks and sitecustomize modules in a Python library directory that your tooling did not install, a detached Python process holding a lock file, and an encrypted archive posted to a path labelled as a health check (Socket, 2026-10-21). In the GitHub organization audit log, short-lived throwaway branches that add a single workflow file, workflow runs deleted minutes after they ran, and branch-protection and force-push-block overrides made with an owner's token; the log records a hash of the token behind each action, which tied the stolen maintainer token to the release approval (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Starting Python or pip in an affected environment can run the payload again, and removing the package directory does not remove the startup files or stop a running loader (Socket, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Rotate every credential the host could reach (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21), because removing the package does not remove the startup files (Socket, 2026-10-21) and stolen cloud credentials were in use within hours (Wiz, 2026-10-21); rebuild from a reviewed release and pin container digests (Socket, 2026-10-21), and move to 1.106.2 or an explicit earlier version as the maintainers advise (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21). For your own pipelines, the root cause was a key that was removed from a public repository's history but never revoked, and an organization owner's CLI token held by an automation service; the maintainers call it an illustration of the risk of failing to rotate a potentially exposed key (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniques

The maintainers published a root-cause post on 2026-10-23 that supersedes the earlier hypothesis that the tokens were read from the logs of an internet-exposed internal deployment: their request logs show the first token came from a different service, an experimental agent platform whose master key had been committed to a public repository on 2026-05-27 and never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The attacker used the key on 2026-10-10 to obtain an organization owner's GitHub CLI token, so access began eleven days before the release, and the same day throwaway branches in two repositories ran workflows that posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint and were deleted minutes later, yielding the tokens of two further maintainers (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

Socket found the same activity independently from the repository's Actions performance metrics, including a second run on 2026-10-12 that took 14 further secrets, and says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 three credentials did different jobs: the owner's token overrode branch protection and later force-pushed the history clean, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate and a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The maintainers say they are revoking every token tied to every internal system and vendor platform, and that the attacker's activity on other systems focused on upstream inference API tokens (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

item.title: Cisco: unauthenticated root RCE on clustered Expressway, fixed only in X15.5.20; X14 and earlier must migrate
item.description: Cisco's disclosure of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 3.1 9.8), which lets an unauthenticated attacker who holds persistent cookies run operating-system commands as root on Expressway-C and Expressway-E that are configured in a cluster; X15.5.3 and earlier get X15.5.20, X14 and earlier must migrate, and there is no workaround. Hardening releases ship the same day for the Unified CM family and Unity Connection (up to 9.8, fixed in 15SU5), and for Snort 3 in Secure Firewall Threat Defense and related products (9.0); Cisco knows of no malicious use of any of them.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-76466 +4NATOA2

CVE-2026-76466, Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E: unauthenticated root command execution on clustered devices, fixed in X15.5.20 with no workaround (CVSS 9.8), alongside same-day hardening releases for Unified CM, Unity Connection and Snort 3

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 3.1 9.8, network, no privileges, no user interaction) in the database service of Expressway-C and Expressway-E, virtual and appliance: an unauthenticated remote attacker with network access can run operating-system commands as root (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). The cause is the use of persistent cookies together with insufficient validation of client certificates for clustering, even when TLS Verify Mode is enabled; an attacker who possesses the cookies connects to the database service and invokes remote procedure call commands, and Cisco does not say how an attacker obtains the cookies (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). Only devices configured in a cluster are affected; X15.5.3 and earlier are fixed in X15.5.20, X14 and earlier must migrate to a fixed release, there is no workaround, and Cisco's PSIRT is not aware of any public announcement or malicious use (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). The X15.5.20 release also carries Expressway's own hardening fixes, whose worst class scores 8.6 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

The same day Cisco ships two further hardening releases whose worst classes are exploitable over the network without authentication. For Emergency Responder, Prime Collaboration Deployment, Unified CM, Unified CM IM&P, Unified CM SME and Unity Connection, regardless of device configuration, the worst classes score 9.8 (CVE-2026-76473, improper control of a resource through its lifetime, and CVE-2026-76474, improper authentication); release 15 is fixed in 15SU5 and release 14 must migrate (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). For Snort 3 in Secure Firewall Threat Defense, Cyber Vision, Unified Threat Defense (UTD) on IOS XE and other Snort-based products, the worst classes score 9.0 with high attack complexity (CVE-2026-20043, an out-of-bounds write, and CVE-2026-20236, an incorrect calculation); FTD is fixed in 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0, Snort in 3.12.4.0, Cyber Vision in 5.6.0 and UTD on IOS XE in 17.12.8, 17.15.6, 17.18.5, 26.1.2 and 26.2.1, while Meraki MX devices that are online and connected to the Dashboard and Cisco's cloud firewall services were updated automatically on 2026-10-21 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). Cisco says the flaws were found during internal security testing using existing processes as well as frontier AI models, and are not known to be actively exploited (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21; Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

Exposure

item.title: GitLab's critical patch fixes an unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 RCE in Org-mode rendering; no exploitation reported
item.description: GitLab's critical patch release of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS 3.1 10.0), an integer overflow in regular-expression handling that lets an unauthenticated user run code on a self-managed GitLab server as the git user; GitLab's own detection write-ups place it in the rendering of .org files, which needs only a public project that can hold the payload. Every version from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, 19.2.9, 19.3.6, 19.4.3 and 19.5.1 is affected, so instances on the 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8 builds that closed the earlier regular-expression flaws still need this release. The bug sits in Ruby's own regular-expression engine, which Ruby fixed on 2026-10-23 in 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13, so any Ruby application that compiles attacker-controlled patterns is exposed to it. GitLab does not report exploitation.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-110264updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-110264, GitLab CE/EE: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the Org-mode renderer's regular-expression handling, fixed in 19.5.1, 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 and backported to four older lines (CVSS 10.0)

GitLab's ad-hoc critical patch release of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS 3.1 10.0), an integer overflow while compiling a specially crafted regular expression that could let an unauthenticated user execute code on the GitLab server (GitLab, 2026-10-21). GitLab's detection write-ups place the flaw in the rendering of Org-mode files: the org-ruby gem builds a regular expression from a custom TODO keyword in a .org file, a keyword with more than 32,767 repeats makes the Onigmo engine write out of bounds when it matches, and with heap grooming that becomes command execution as the git user (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). The attack needs no authentication, only one public project that can hold the .org payload (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). Affected are all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9, 19.2 before 19.2.9, 19.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3 and 19.5 before 19.5.1; GitLab.com is already patched, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0 or later need no action (GitLab, 2026-10-21). The builds 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8 from GitLab's earlier regular-expression fixes do not contain this fix (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). GitLab does not state that the flaw is exploited, and its patch notes and detection pages mention no public proof of concept (GitLab, 2026-10-21). The bug is in Ruby's Onigmo regular-expression engine: the Ruby project released 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 on 2026-10-23 with the fix, the release of 4.0.8 lacks the fix for this flaw, and GitLab fixed its own servers by patching the Ruby it ships (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

Exposure
Self-managed GitLab CE and EE on the versions above; the vulnerable path is reached when GitLab renders a .org file, so an instance with public projects, or one where untrusted users can create them, is the exposed shape, and until patching GitLab advises reducing public visibility (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). A Ruby application outside GitLab is exposed to the same bug when it compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls, through Regexp.new, Regexp.union, Regexp.compile or interpolation into a regexp literal; applications that only use patterns written by their own developers are not affected (Ruby, 2026-10-23).
Detection
GitLab's two detections key on, first, five or more render timeouts from the Org-mode renderer on .org files from one client within 30 minutes in the Rails exceptions log, with the request that actually crashes a worker visible only as a 502 on the .org blob route in the Workhorse log, and second, a native Ruby crash report in the Puma error log whose backtrace runs through org-ruby or Onigmo frames (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). In repository content, scan each suspect checkout for .org files with an oversized TODO-keyword line, and in the Rails request log look for editor preview requests whose file_path ends in .org while the URL names another file type, which forces the Org renderer (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). A successful exploit is quiet and does not reliably crash, so the absence of a hit never clears an instance (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). On an exposed, unpatched instance, hunt for unexpected child processes of Puma, new files owned by git in the temporary directory, outbound connections and changed crontabs or SSH keys for the git user, and treat the secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens and access tokens the git user can read as at risk (GitLab security, 2026-10-21).

Triage: a reader of documentation .org files renders each file once and quickly, while an attack produces a burst of timeouts from one client over a few minutes (GitLab security, 2026-10-21); a worker crash with no accompanying render burst from one client is more likely a benign parser bug than an attack (GitLab security, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to the fixed build of the instance's line now, internet-reachable instances and those with public projects first; an instance that moved to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 for the earlier flaws is not yet fixed for this one (GitLab, 2026-10-21). For other Ruby applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns, Ruby recommends upgrading to 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13 or later, or avoiding compiling such patterns, and says neither Regexp.timeout nor a pattern-length limit reliably protects; Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own for now and tells operators to track the issues under GitLab's identifiers (Ruby, 2026-10-23).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelaffected_productsbodycvesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummaryentities

The Ruby project published an advisory on 2026-10-23 and released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 with fixes for the bugs in its Onigmo regular-expression engine behind four GitLab flaws: CVE-2026-89078 (a double free when parsing a pattern fails after an alternation), CVE-2026-93577 and CVE-2026-97229 (an integer overflow in the size of a compiled pattern) and CVE-2026-110264 (an overflow of internal IDs in a pattern with many repeats) (Ruby, 2026-10-23). Ruby's table gives the first release of each series that carries each fix: the fix for CVE-2026-110264 first appears in 4.0.9, so 4.0.8 is not enough, and 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 carry all of them; GitLab fixed its own servers by patching the Ruby it ships (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

The advisory widens the exposure beyond GitLab to any Ruby application that compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls, says Regexp.timeout does not protect against these bugs and that limiting pattern length does not reliably protect, and says Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own and that operators should track the issues under GitLab's identifiers (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

item.title: Palo Alto: PHP2Shell affects PAN-OS and Panorama; PAN-OS hotfixes due 26 to 30 October
item.description: Palo Alto Networks' advisory of 2026-10-21, revised on 2026-10-24, lists every release of PAN-OS 12.2, 12.1, 11.2, 11.1 and 10.2 as affected by the two PHP runtime flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and notes that the issue applies to PAN-OS software on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama; no fixed build is released, hotfixes for each PAN-OS train carry estimated dates from 2026-10-26 to 2026-10-30, and the table no longer distinguishes Panorama, which the note and the mitigation text cover together with PAN-OS. The WildFire appliances WF-500 and WF-500-B, which an earlier revision of 2026-10-23 listed as affected, are now listed as unaffected after a correction its timeline dates 2026-10-23. Cortex XCORE (SaaS) and WildFire Cloud were already remediated. The PAN-OS exposure is the management web interface (the HTTPS web UI and the XML API service); Palo Alto scores the PAN-OS impact as availability only, CVSS-B 8.7 where management is reachable from the internet and 7.1 behind a jump box, against 9.2 for the PHP flaws themselves, and knows of no malicious exploitation against its products. GlobalProtect and the captive portal are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-109618 +1updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Panorama: the PHP2Shell flaws affect every release, reaching PAN-OS through its management web interface; PAN-OS hotfixes are scheduled for 2026-10-26 to 2026-10-30

Palo Alto Networks' advisory of 2026-10-21 lists every release of PAN-OS 12.2, 12.1, 11.2, 11.1 and 10.2 and of Panorama as affected by CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, with no fixed build released (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21); the revision of 2026-10-23 gave estimated dates from 2026-10-26 to 2026-10-30 for hotfix builds of every PAN-OS train and noted that Cortex XCORE (SaaS) and WildFire Cloud were remediated on 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22 (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-23). The advisory's timeline dates a correction of the WildFire appliances WF-500 and WF-500-B to 2026-10-23, and the table now lists them as unaffected, although the revision that morning had listed them as affected; the table no longer distinguishes Panorama, a note says the issue applies to PAN-OS software on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama (virtual and M-Series), and the mitigation text covers PAN-OS and Panorama together (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24). The revision of 2026-10-24 added updated threat-signature and content-version details (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24). The two flaws are the unauthenticated remote-code-execution bugs in the PHP runtime that the PHP project fixed in its releases of the same day (PHP, 2026-10-21). Palo Alto says no special configuration is required to be affected, that the issue strictly affects the management web interface, which includes the HTTPS web UI and the XML API service, and that a dataplane interface is affected only where a management profile is attached to it (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21). It states that the GlobalProtect portal and gateway and the captive portal are not impacted (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).

Palo Alto describes the flaws as remote code execution but scores their impact on its own product CVSS-B 8.7 (severity high, urgency moderate), with high availability impact and none on confidentiality or integrity, against a vendor-level 9.2 with high impact on all three, and says the risk is highest where management access is allowed from external addresses on the internet; restricting management to a single jump box lowers its rating to 7.1, and it is not aware of any malicious exploitation against its products (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21). Unit 42 says it has seen proof of concept of the PHP flaws (Unit 42, 2026-10-21). Until fixes ship, Palo Alto recommends restricting management access to trusted internal addresses and offers Threat Prevention coverage (Threat IDs 543004 and 97622 to 97625 and twenty further IDs from 97643 to 97678, Applications and Threats content versions 9162, 9163, 9164 and later) that applies only when management traffic is routed through a dataplane interface, the certificate for inbound management traffic has been replaced, inbound management traffic is decrypted so the firewall can inspect it, and threat prevention is enabled on that traffic (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24).

Exposure
Every PAN-OS firewall and Panorama appliance, whatever the configuration, through its management web interface; the service is reachable from the internet where the management port, or a dataplane interface carrying a management profile, answers HTTPS or XML API requests from outside the administrator range (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In management-plane access and system logs, any request from an address outside the administrator range, though Palo Alto does not say which logs record request bodies; in threat logs, hits on the Threat IDs above where the signatures are active and the four conditions hold. Palo Alto publishes no flaw-specific indicator and reports no exploitation of its products, so no post-compromise check is defined yet (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Move management access behind a jump box or trusted internal addresses now, and remove management profiles from dataplane interfaces that face untrusted networks; Palo Alto lists no workaround beyond that restriction and the Threat Prevention coverage; its revision of 2026-10-23 schedules the first PAN-OS hotfixes for 2026-10-26 (10.2.18-h13, 11.1.16-h4 and 11.2.10-h16) and the rest by 2026-10-30, so install the hotfix of each train when it is released, while the advisory's note and mitigation text cover PAN-OS and Panorama together and its table no longer distinguishes Panorama, so apply the same management-access restriction to Panorama (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-24).
